Do the movements occur when your hand is completely at rest?
Do they disappear when you are asleep?
Are the movements confined mainly to one hand or one side of your body?
Do you feel an urge or inner sensation that is relieved by making the movement?
Are the movements worse when you are anxious, concentrating, or being watched?
Can touching or changing the position of your hand temporarily reduce the movements?
Do you have stiffness, slowness, or a resting tremor elsewhere?
Have you noticed weakness, numbness, loss of coordination, or clumsiness on that side?
Have you had any recent stroke, head injury, infection, or other brain illness?
Do you take levodopa, antipsychotic medication, nausea medication, or other dopamine-blocking medication?
Have you ever been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease or another movement disorder?
Do you have involuntary movements of your mouth, tongue, face, legs, or the other hand?

results: 1. skin examination: a painless, non-pruritic confluent erythematous rash on the left arm one day before the chorea began; it improved with doxycycline and clindamycin but the chorea did not
2. autoimmune encephalopathy / paraneoplastic antibody panel: NEGATIVE in serum and CSF - seronegative
3. brain MRI with contrast: 1.5T with gadolinium - frontal-predominant atrophy but NO focal lesion, with normal basal ganglia structure and volume
4. PET-CT or CT body (occult malignancy): skull base to thighs - no malignancy and no infection
5. trial of immunotherapy: empirical IVIg produced DRAMATIC improvement of the hemichorea - the diagnosis rests on the treatment response
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Seronegative post-infectious autoimmune hemichorea, most likely triggered by the preceding left-arm bacterial skin infection/cellulitis

Sydenham chorea

Seronegative paraneoplastic autoimmune chorea

Huntington disease or another neurodegenerative chorea
